papers.short_title: CATIE Trial — Antipsychotic Effectiveness in Schizophrenia
papers.primary_citation: Lieberman JA, Stroup TS, McEvoy JP, et al. "Effectiveness of Antipsychotic Drugs in Patients with Chronic Schizophrenia." New England Journal of Medicine. 2005;353(12):1209–1223. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa051688. PubMed: 16172203
papers.practice_changing: Yes — fundamentally changed how clinicians think about antipsychotic selection.
papers.why_matters: The NIMH-funded CATIE trial (N=1,460, 57 US sites, 18 months) shattered the prevailing assumption that second-generation antipsychotics were categorically superior to first-generation agents. Perphenazine performed comparably to quetiapine, risperidone, and ziprasidone, while olanzapine had the longest time to discontinuation but the worst metabolic profile. Only 26% of patients completed 18 months on their initial medication, revealing the profound challenge of long-term antipsychotic treatment.[1]
papers.key_findings: 74% discontinued before 18 months (median 4.6 months). Olanzapine had the longest time to discontinuation (9.2 months) but caused the most weight gain and metabolic effects. In Phase 2, clozapine was superior to other SGAs for patients who failed Phase 1 due to lack of efficacy.[1]
clinical_pearls: The FGA/SGA distinction is pharmacologically misleading — choose antipsychotics based on individual side-effect profiles, not class
Metabolic monitoring is essential for all antipsychotics, especially olanzapine
Expect medication changes — most patients will not remain on their first antipsychotic long-term
Clozapine remains the gold standard for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
Effectiveness (real-world outcomes) matters more than efficacy (controlled trial results)
papers.recommended_follow_up: Huhn et al. "Comparative Efficacy and Tolerability of 32 Oral Antipsychotics." Lancet. 2019.[2]

papers.short_title: Kane et al. — Clozapine for Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia
papers.primary_citation: Kane J, Honigfeld G, Singer J, Meltzer H. "Clozapine for the Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenic: A Double-Blind Comparison with Chlorpromazine." Archives of General Psychiatry. 1988;45(9):789–796. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.1988.01800330013001. PubMed: 3046553
papers.practice_changing: Yes — clozapine remains the standard of care for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
papers.why_matters: This landmark trial established clozapine as the only antipsychotic with demonstrated superiority in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. After a rigorous haloperidol lead-in to confirm treatment resistance, 30% of clozapine patients responded versus only 4% on chlorpromazine (p<0.001). The effect size (SMD −0.88) has never been replicated in subsequent trials, and clozapine remains the only FDA-approved medication for this indication.[3][4]
papers.key_findings: Response rate 30% vs. 4% (p<0.001); mean BPRS change −16 vs. −5 (p<0.001). Defined treatment resistance as failure of ≥3 adequate antipsychotic trials.[3]
clinical_pearls: Clozapine should be offered after failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials — delays in initiation are common and harmful
Requires absolute neutrophil count (ANC) monitoring due to agranulocytosis risk (~1%)
Clozapine is also the only antipsychotic FDA-approved for reducing suicidal behavior in schizophrenia (InterSePT trial)[5]
Associated with the lowest mortality of any antipsychotic in large cohort studies[6]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Samara et al. "Efficacy, Acceptability, and Tolerability of Antipsychotics in Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia: A Network Meta-Analysis." JAMA Psychiatry. 2016.[4]

papers.short_title: STARD — Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression
papers.primary_citation: Rush AJ, Trivedi MH, Wisniewski SR, et al. "Acute and Longer-Term Outcomes in Depressed Outpatients Requiring One or Several Treatment Steps: A STARD Report." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2006;163(11):1905–1917. doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.163.11.1905. PubMed: 17074942
papers.practice_changing: Yes — established measurement-based care and realistic expectations for depression treatment.
papers.why_matters: The largest depression treatment effectiveness study ever conducted (N=4,041, 41 sites) demonstrated that real-world remission rates are far lower than controlled trials suggest. Step 1 citalopram remission was ~37%; cumulative remission across four steps was reported as 67%, though a 2023 reanalysis using protocol-stipulated blinded outcomes estimated ~35%. No antidepressant was clearly superior to another at any step. STARD also pioneered measurement-based care in real-world settings.[7][8][9]
papers.key_findings: Remission rates declined with each step (37%, 31%, 14%, 13%). Relapse rates increased with each step. Patients who achieved remission had lower relapse rates than those who achieved only response (34% vs. 59% at Step 1).[7]
clinical_pearls: Remission, not response, should be the treatment target — it predicts better long-term outcomes
Use measurement-based care (PHQ-9, QIDS) to guide treatment decisions systematically
If the first antidepressant fails, switching within or between classes is reasonable — no switch strategy is clearly superior
Augmentation with bupropion may be slightly more effective than buspirone augmentation
Most patients will need more than one treatment trial
papers.recommended_follow_up: Pigott et al. "What Are the Treatment Remission, Response and Extent of Improvement Rates After Up to Four Trials of Antidepressant Therapies?" BMJ Open. 2023.[9]

papers.short_title: Cipriani et al. — Comparative Efficacy of 21 Antidepressants
papers.primary_citation: Cipriani A, Furukawa TA, Salanti G, et al. "Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of 21 Antidepressant Drugs for the Acute Treatment of Adults with Major Depressive Disorder: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis." Lancet. 2018;391(10128):1357–1366. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32802-7. PubMed: 29477251
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the definitive reference for antidepressant selection.
papers.why_matters: The largest network meta-analysis of antidepressants ever conducted (522 RCTs, 116,477 participants) definitively demonstrated that all 21 antidepressants were more effective than placebo, settling a long-standing public debate. It also provided the first comprehensive head-to-head efficacy and acceptability rankings, with agomelatine, amitriptyline, escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine, and vortioxetine showing the best efficacy profiles.[10]
papers.key_findings: ORs for efficacy ranged from 2.13 (amitriptyline) to 1.37 (reboxetine). For acceptability, agomelatine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline, and vortioxetine were most tolerable.[10]
clinical_pearls: Antidepressants work — the debate about whether they are better than placebo is settled
Escitalopram and sertraline offer the best balance of efficacy and tolerability
Amitriptyline is the most efficacious but has the worst side-effect profile
Choice should be individualized based on side-effect profile, cost, patient preference, and comorbidities
Effect sizes are modest (OR ~1.5–2.0), meaning many patients will not respond to any single agent
papers.recommended_follow_up: Park & Zarate. "Depression in the Primary Care Setting." NEJM. 2019.[11]

papers.short_title: Inouye et al. — The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)
papers.primary_citation: Inouye SK, van Dyck CH, Alessi CA, et al. "Clarifying Confusion: The Confusion Assessment Method." Annals of Internal Medicine. 1990;113(12):941–948. doi:10.7326/0003-4819-113-12-941. PubMed: 2240918
papers.practice_changing: Yes — remains the standard delirium screening tool worldwide.
papers.why_matters: The CAM is the most widely used delirium screening instrument in the world, cited in >4,500 studies and translated into 19 languages. Its four-feature algorithm (acute onset/fluctuating course + inattention + either disorganized thinking or altered consciousness) achieves 94–100% sensitivity and 90–95% specificity in <5 minutes. This paper transformed delirium from an underrecognized condition to a routinely screened syndrome.[12][13]
papers.key_findings: Sensitivity 94–100%, specificity 90–95%, interrater reliability κ = 0.81–1.0. Validated in 56 subjects aged 65–98.[12]
clinical_pearls: Delirium is present in 10–30% of hospitalized medical patients — screen actively
Inattention is the cardinal feature; if the patient can attend normally, delirium is unlikely
The CAM requires training to administer reliably — untrained users have lower sensitivity
Always distinguish delirium from dementia and depression (the "3 D's")
Hypoactive delirium is more common than hyperactive and more frequently missed
papers.recommended_follow_up: Marcantonio. "Delirium in Hospitalized Older Adults." NEJM. 2017.[14]

papers.short_title: Inouye et al. — Yale Delirium Prevention Trial (HELP)
papers.primary_citation: Inouye SK, Bogardus ST, Charpentier PA, et al. "A Multicomponent Intervention to Prevent Delirium in Hospitalized Older Patients." New England Journal of Medicine. 1999;340(9):669–676. doi:10.1056/NEJM199903043400901. PubMed: 10053175
papers.practice_changing: Yes — HELP remains the evidence-based standard for delirium prevention.
papers.why_matters: This landmark trial established that multicomponent nonpharmacologic prevention is the most effective strategy for reducing delirium. The Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP) targeted six modifiable risk factors using a trained interdisciplinary team. A subsequent meta-analysis of 14 HELP-based studies demonstrated a 53% reduction in delirium incidence (OR 0.47) and 62% reduction in falls.[15][16]
papers.key_findings: Delirium incidence reduced from 15% to 9.9% (matched OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39–0.92). Total number of delirium days and episodes also significantly reduced.[15]
clinical_pearls: Delirium prevention is more effective than treatment — implement HELP-based protocols
Target modifiable risk factors: reorient frequently, mobilize early, correct sensory deficits, avoid unnecessary medications, maintain hydration, promote sleep hygiene
No pharmacologic agent has been shown to prevent delirium
The predisposing + precipitating factors model explains why some patients develop delirium and others do not[17][18]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Oh et al. "Delirium in Older Persons: Advances in Diagnosis and Treatment." JAMA. 2017.[13]

papers.short_title: Linehan — Dialectical Behavior Therapy for Borderline Personality Disorder
papers.primary_citation: Linehan MM, Armstrong HE, Suarez A, Allmon D, Heard HL. "Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment of Chronically Parasuicidal Borderline Patients." Archives of General Psychiatry. 1991;48(12):1060–1064. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.1991.01810360024003. PubMed: 1845222
papers.practice_changing: Yes — DBT remains the most evidence-based treatment for BPD.
papers.why_matters: The first RCT of DBT demonstrated that a structured psychotherapy could significantly reduce parasuicidal behavior and hospitalization in women with BPD — a population previously considered "untreatable." DBT's four-module structure (individual therapy, group skills training, telephone coaching, team consultation) became the template for evidence-based personality disorder treatment. A 2017 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis confirmed DBT as one of only two psychotherapy types (alongside psychodynamic approaches) significantly more effective than controls for BPD outcomes.[19][20]
papers.key_findings: DBT reduced parasuicidal acts, inpatient psychiatric days, and treatment dropout compared to treatment as usual over 1 year.[19]
clinical_pearls: BPD is treatable — structured psychotherapy produces meaningful improvement
DBT skills (distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness, mindfulness) are useful across diagnoses
On inpatient units, DBT-informed approaches (validation + change strategies) reduce behavioral crises
Avoid the "splitting" trap — maintain consistent team communication about BPD patients
A 2025 RCT showed DBT produced significantly fewer suicide-related events than SSRI/clinical management[21]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Bohus et al. "Borderline Personality Disorder." Lancet. 2021.[22]

papers.short_title: STEP-BD — Antidepressants in Bipolar Depression
papers.primary_citation: Sachs GS, Nierenberg AA, Calabrese JR, et al. "Effectiveness of Adjunctive Antidepressant Treatment for Bipolar Depression." New England Journal of Medicine. 2007;356(17):1711–1722. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa064135. PubMed: 17460148
papers.practice_changing: Yes — guides current bipolar depression management.
papers.why_matters: This NIMH-funded RCT within the STEP-BD program (N=366) definitively showed that adjunctive antidepressants (paroxetine or bupropion) added to mood stabilizers were no more effective than placebo for bipolar depression (durable recovery 23.5% vs. 27.3%, p=0.40). Equally important, antidepressants did not increase the risk of treatment-emergent affective switch. This trial fundamentally changed the approach to bipolar depression treatment.[23]
papers.key_findings: No efficacy advantage for antidepressants; no increased switch risk. Durable recovery rates were low in both groups (~25%), highlighting the difficulty of treating bipolar depression.[23]
clinical_pearls: Do not reflexively add antidepressants for bipolar depression — they may not help
Optimize mood stabilizer therapy first (lithium, lamotrigine, quetiapine)
Always screen for bipolarity before starting antidepressants for depression
Bipolar depression is harder to treat than bipolar mania — set realistic expectations
Intensive psychotherapy (CBT, IPSRT, FFT) improved recovery rates to 64% vs. 52% in the companion STEP-BD psychotherapy trial[24]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Yatham et al. "CANMAT and ISBD 2018 Guidelines for Management of Patients with Bipolar Disorder." Bipolar Disorders. 2018.

papers.short_title: Cipriani et al. — Lithium and Suicide Prevention
papers.primary_citation: Cipriani A, Hawton K, Stockton S, Geddes JR. "Lithium in the Prevention of Suicide in Mood Disorders: Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." BMJ. 2013;346:f3646. doi:10.1136/bmj.f3646. PubMed: 23814104
papers.practice_changing: Yes — lithium remains the only medication with robust evidence for suicide prevention.
papers.why_matters: This meta-analysis of 48 RCTs (6,674 participants) provided the strongest evidence that lithium reduces completed suicides (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03–0.66) and all-cause mortality (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.15–0.95) in mood disorders. No other psychotropic medication has demonstrated this effect with comparable strength. This finding has made lithium a cornerstone of suicide prevention in bipolar disorder and recurrent depression.[25]
papers.key_findings: Lithium reduced suicides by 87% and all-cause mortality by 62% compared to placebo. Lithium also reduced deliberate self-harm (OR 0.36).[25]
clinical_pearls: Lithium's anti-suicidal effect appears independent of its mood-stabilizing properties
Consider lithium preferentially in patients with mood disorders and suicidal ideation/history
The anti-suicide effect requires ongoing treatment — abrupt discontinuation increases risk[26]
Lithium levels, renal function, and thyroid function require regular monitoring
A Swedish within-individual study confirmed lithium (but not valproate) reduced suicide-related events by 14%[27]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Song et al. "Suicidal Behavior During Lithium and Valproate Treatment." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2017.[27]

papers.short_title: Mann et al. — Suicide Prevention Strategies
papers.primary_citation: Mann JJ, Apter A, Bertolote J, et al. "Suicide Prevention Strategies: A Systematic Review." JAMA. 2005;294(16):2064–2074. doi:10.1001/jama.294.16.2064. PubMed: 16249421
papers.practice_changing: Yes — means restriction and safety planning are now standard of care.
papers.why_matters: This international expert review identified physician education in depression recognition/treatment and restricting access to lethal means as the only two suicide prevention strategies with strong evidence for reducing suicide rates. It established the evidence-based framework for suicide prevention that remains current today.[28]
papers.key_findings: Means restriction (firearms, pesticides, bridge barriers, medication packaging) consistently reduces suicide rates without compensatory method substitution. Physician education programs reduced suicide rates in controlled studies.[28]
clinical_pearls: Always ask about access to firearms and other lethal means — and counsel on safe storage
Means restriction works because many suicidal crises are brief and impulsive
Most people who survive a suicide attempt do not go on to die by suicide
Screening for depression in primary care, combined with treatment, reduces suicide
The Safety Planning Intervention (Stanley & Brown) halved suicidal behavior in ED patients[29]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Mann et al. "Improving Suicide Prevention Through Evidence-Based Strategies." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2021.[30]

papers.short_title: Posner et al. — Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS)
papers.primary_citation: Posner K, Brown GK, Stanley B, et al. "The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale: Initial Validity and Internal Consistency Findings from Three Multisite Studies with Adolescents and Adults." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2011;168(12):1266–1277. doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.2011.10111704. PubMed: 22193671
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the standard suicide assessment tool.
papers.why_matters: The C-SSRS provided the first validated, standardized instrument that distinguishes suicidal ideation from suicidal behavior and grades ideation severity on a 5-point scale. It has become the predominant suicide risk assessment tool in clinical practice, research, and regulatory settings. A 2025 meta-analysis confirmed its predictive validity: suicidal behavior predicted future non-fatal attempts (pooled OR 3.14).[31][32]
papers.key_findings: Good convergent/divergent validity across three multisite studies. Worst-point lifetime suicidal ideation predicted future suicide attempts, whereas the Scale for Suicide Ideation did not.[31]
clinical_pearls: Use the C-SSRS to systematically assess suicidal ideation intensity, duration, and associated behaviors
Distinguish passive ideation ("I wish I were dead") from active ideation with intent and plan
Prior suicidal behavior is the strongest predictor of future attempts
The C-SSRS is required by the FDA for all clinical trials involving psychiatric medications
Pair C-SSRS assessment with the Safety Planning Intervention for actionable risk management
papers.recommended_follow_up: Stanley et al. "Comparison of the Safety Planning Intervention with Follow-Up vs Usual Care." JAMA Psychiatry. 2018.[29]

papers.short_title: Bush et al. — Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale and Lorazepam Treatment
papers.primary_citation: Bush G, Fink M, Petrides G, Dowling F, Francis A. "Catatonia. I. Rating Scale and Standardized Examination" and "Catatonia. II. Treatment with Lorazepam and Electroconvulsive Therapy." Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica. 1996;93(2):129–143. doi:10.1111/j.1600-0447.1996.tb09814.x. PubMed: 8686483
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the BFCRS and lorazepam challenge are current standard of care.
papers.why_matters: These companion papers established the BFCRS as the standard catatonia assessment instrument and operationalized the lorazepam challenge test. The 23-item scale (14-item screening version) captures all DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria. In the treatment study, 76% of catatonic patients responded completely to lorazepam, and all lorazepam non-responders responded to ECT. This created the modern treatment algorithm: lorazepam first → ECT for non-responders.[33][34]
papers.key_findings: BFCRS screening score ≥2 is positive. Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV produces response in 66–100% of cases, often within minutes. ECT response rate 60–100% in lorazepam non-responders.[33][35]
clinical_pearls: Screen for catatonia in any patient with psychomotor abnormalities — it is underdiagnosed
The lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV, reassess BFCRS at 1–2 hours) is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Catatonia occurs in medical, neurological, and psychiatric conditions — not just schizophrenia
Avoid antipsychotics in catatonia — they can worsen symptoms and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome
NMS and malignant catatonia may represent the same spectrum[36]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Heckers & Walther. "Catatonia." NEJM. 2023.[36]

papers.short_title: UK ECT Review Group — ECT Efficacy Meta-Analysis
papers.primary_citation: UK ECT Review Group. "Efficacy and Safety of Electroconvulsive Therapy in Depressive Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." Lancet. 2003;361(9360):799–808. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(03)12705-5. PubMed: 12642045
papers.practice_changing: Yes — ECT remains the most effective treatment for severe depression.
papers.why_matters: This remains the most comprehensive meta-analysis of ECT efficacy, demonstrating that ECT is significantly more effective than sham ECT and probably more effective than pharmacotherapy for depression (mean difference 5.2 HDRS points). It also established that bilateral ECT is moderately more effective than unilateral, and high-dose more effective than low-dose.[37]
papers.key_findings: ECT superior to sham ECT (6 trials) and to pharmacotherapy (18 trials). Bilateral > unilateral; high-dose > low-dose. Response rates 60–80% for treatment-resistant depression.[37][38]
clinical_pearls: ECT is the most effective acute treatment for severe depression — do not reserve it as a "last resort"
Indications include severe depression with psychotic features, catatonia, acute suicidality, and treatment resistance
Nearly all patients relapse without continuation treatment — plan post-ECT pharmacotherapy or continuation ECT[39]
Cognitive side effects (primarily autobiographical memory) are real but usually transient
Right unilateral ultra-brief pulse ECT minimizes cognitive effects while maintaining efficacy
papers.recommended_follow_up: Espinoza & Kellner. "Electroconvulsive Therapy." NEJM. 2022.[38]

papers.short_title: BALANCE Trial — Lithium vs. Valproate for Bipolar Maintenance
papers.primary_citation: BALANCE Investigators, Geddes JR, Goodwin GM, et al. "Lithium Plus Valproate Combination Therapy Versus Monotherapy for Relapse Prevention in Bipolar I Disorder (BALANCE): A Randomised Open-Label Trial." Lancet. 2010;375(9712):385–395. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(09)61828-6. PubMed: 20092882
papers.practice_changing: Yes — supports lithium as first-line maintenance therapy.
papers.why_matters: This multicenter RCT (N=330) demonstrated that lithium monotherapy and lithium + valproate combination were significantly more effective than valproate monotherapy for preventing relapse in bipolar I disorder (HR 0.71 for lithium vs. valproate). This reinforced lithium's position as the first-line mood stabilizer and challenged the growing trend of substituting valproate for lithium.[40]
papers.key_findings: Lithium monotherapy and combination therapy were superior to valproate monotherapy. Lithium's advantage was most apparent for depressive relapses (HR 0.63).[40]
clinical_pearls: Lithium should be the first-line mood stabilizer for bipolar I disorder
Valproate monotherapy is inferior to lithium for maintenance — do not substitute without reason
Combination therapy (lithium + valproate) may be appropriate for patients with incomplete response
Gradual lithium discontinuation is essential — abrupt withdrawal precipitates relapse (median 4 months vs. 20 months)[26]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Miura et al. "Comparative Efficacy and Tolerability of Pharmacological Treatments in the Maintenance Treatment of Bipolar Disorder." Lancet Psychiatry. 2014.[41]

papers.short_title: Unützer et al. — IMPACT Trial (Collaborative Care)
papers.primary_citation: Unützer J, Katon W, Callahan CM, et al. "Collaborative Care Management of Late-Life Depression in the Primary Care Setting: A Randomized Controlled Trial." JAMA. 2002;288(22):2836–2845. doi:10.1001/jama.288.22.2836. PubMed: 12472325
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the dominant model for integrated behavioral health.
papers.why_matters: The IMPACT trial (N=1,801, 18 clinics, 8 health systems) demonstrated that collaborative care — a depression care manager supervised by a psychiatrist, offering education, care management, and brief psychotherapy — more than doubled the effectiveness of depression treatment in primary care (45% vs. 19% response at 12 months, OR 3.45). This became the foundational evidence for the collaborative care model now endorsed by CMS and implemented across health systems.[42][43]
papers.key_findings: 50% depression symptom reduction: 45% intervention vs. 19% usual care (OR 3.45). Benefits sustained at 18 and 24 months. Equally effective in Black and Latino patients.[42][44]
clinical_pearls: Collaborative care is the most evidence-based model for integrating psychiatry into primary care
The model requires three elements: a care manager, a consulting psychiatrist, and a registry/tracking system
Psychiatrists can extend their reach dramatically through consultation rather than direct care alone
A Cochrane review of 79 RCTs confirmed collaborative care's effectiveness (SMD −0.34)[45]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Archer et al. "Collaborative Care for Depression and Anxiety Problems." Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012.[45]

papers.short_title: Hammad et al. — FDA Antidepressant Black Box Warning
papers.primary_citation: Hammad TA, Laughren T, Racoosin J. "Suicidality in Pediatric Patients Treated with Antidepressant Drugs." Archives of General Psychiatry. 2006;63(3):332–339. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.63.3.332. PubMed: 16520440
papers.practice_changing: Yes — shapes every antidepressant prescription in youth.
papers.why_matters: This FDA meta-analysis of 24 RCTs (>4,400 pediatric patients) found that antidepressants approximately doubled the risk of suicidal ideation/behavior (RR 1.95, 95% CI 1.28–2.98), with no completed suicides. This led to the 2004 black box warning — the most consequential regulatory action in psychopharmacology. However, the warning had profound unintended consequences: antidepressant prescribing dropped 31% in adolescents, while suicide attempts increased 21.7%.[46][47]
papers.key_findings: RR 1.95 for suicidal ideation/behavior; no completed suicides. Bridge et al. (2007) subsequently showed the NNH was 143 while the NNT was 10 for MDD, concluding benefits far outweigh risks.[46][48]
clinical_pearls: The black box warning is real but must be contextualized — untreated depression carries greater suicide risk
Monitor closely during the first 4–8 weeks of antidepressant treatment, especially in youth
Combining antidepressants with CBT may protect against treatment-emergent suicidality (TADS finding)[49]
Fluoxetine is the best-studied and first-line antidepressant for adolescent depression
The warning's unintended consequences illustrate how well-intentioned policies can cause harm[47]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Bridge et al. "Clinical Response and Risk for Reported Suicidal Ideation and Suicide Attempts in Pediatric Antidepressant Treatment." JAMA. 2007.[48]

papers.short_title: ADA/APA Consensus — Metabolic Monitoring for Antipsychotics
papers.primary_citation: American Diabetes Association, American Psychiatric Association, et al. "Consensus Development Conference on Antipsychotic Drugs and Obesity and Diabetes." Diabetes Care. 2004;27(2):596–601. doi:10.2337/diacare.27.2.596. PubMed: 14747245
papers.practice_changing: Yes — metabolic monitoring is standard of care.
papers.why_matters: This joint consensus statement established the first standardized metabolic monitoring protocol for patients on second-generation antipsychotics, including baseline and follow-up assessments of weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose, and fasting lipids. It also described the differential metabolic risk hierarchy among SGAs. Despite its importance, adherence to these guidelines has remained disappointingly low.[50][51]
papers.key_findings: Clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole and ziprasidone the lowest. Monitoring protocol: baseline assessment, then weight at 4, 8, and 12 weeks, glucose/lipids at 12 weeks and annually.[50][52]
clinical_pearls: Every patient starting an antipsychotic needs baseline metabolic labs — this is non-negotiable
Olanzapine and clozapine require the most vigilant metabolic monitoring
Weight gain often occurs rapidly in the first 6–12 weeks — intervene early
Consider switching to a metabolically neutral agent (aripiprazole, ziprasidone) if significant weight gain occurs
Pillinger et al. (2020) confirmed these risk hierarchies in a network meta-analysis of 100 RCTs[53]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Pillinger et al. "Comparative Effects of 18 Antipsychotics on Metabolic Function." Lancet Psychiatry. 2020.[53]

papers.short_title: RAISE-ETP — Coordinated Specialty Care for First-Episode Psychosis
papers.primary_citation: Kane JM, Robinson DG, Schooler NR, et al. "Comprehensive Versus Usual Community Care for First-Episode Psychosis: 2-Year Outcomes from the NIMH RAISE Early Treatment Program." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2016;173(4):362–372. doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.2015.15050632. PubMed: 26481174
papers.practice_changing: Yes — coordinated specialty care is now the standard for first-episode psychosis.
papers.why_matters: This NIMH-funded cluster-randomized trial (N=404, 34 US clinics) demonstrated that coordinated specialty care (NAVIGATE program) for first-episode psychosis improved quality of life, psychopathology, and work/school involvement compared to usual community care. Effects were most pronounced when duration of untreated psychosis was <74 weeks. This trial led to NIMH's national dissemination of coordinated specialty care programs.[54]
papers.key_findings: NAVIGATE participants remained in treatment longer, had greater improvement in quality of life and symptoms, and greater involvement in work/school. Five-year follow-up supported sustained benefit.[54][55]
clinical_pearls: First-episode psychosis is a critical window — early, comprehensive intervention improves long-term outcomes
Coordinated specialty care includes low-dose antipsychotics, individual therapy, family education, and supported employment/education
Duration of untreated psychosis (DUP) is a modifiable prognostic factor — reduce delays to treatment
Many first-episode patients can be managed on lower antipsychotic doses than chronic patients
papers.recommended_follow_up: Correll et al. "Comparison of Early Intervention Services vs Treatment as Usual for Early-Phase Psychosis." JAMA Psychiatry. 2018.[56]

papers.short_title: Leucht et al. — Antipsychotic Maintenance Treatment Meta-Analysis
papers.primary_citation: Leucht S, Tardy M, Komossa K, et al. "Antipsychotic Drugs Versus Placebo for Relapse Prevention in Schizophrenia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." Lancet. 2012;379(9831):2063–2071. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(12)60239-6. PubMed: 22560607
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the definitive evidence for maintenance antipsychotic treatment.
papers.why_matters: This meta-analysis of 65 RCTs (6,493 participants) provided the definitive evidence that maintenance antipsychotic treatment reduces 1-year relapse from 64% (placebo) to 27% (NNT=3). It also showed that depot/long-acting injectable formulations reduced relapse more than oral medications (RR 0.31 vs. 0.46). This settled the debate about whether antipsychotics should be continued long-term.[57]
papers.key_findings: Relapse reduction from 64% to 27% (RR 0.40, NNT=3). Depot > oral (p=0.03). Also improved quality of life and reduced aggressive acts.[57]
clinical_pearls: Maintenance antipsychotic treatment is essential — the NNT of 3 is among the strongest in medicine
Long-acting injectables should be offered early, not reserved as a "last resort"
Discuss the relapse data with patients to support shared decision-making about continuation
Even with treatment, 27% relapse at 1 year — adjunctive psychosocial interventions are important
papers.recommended_follow_up: Tiihonen et al. "Real-World Effectiveness of Antipsychotic Treatments in a Nationwide Cohort." JAMA Psychiatry. 2017.[58]

papers.short_title: TADS — Treatment for Adolescents with Depression Study
papers.primary_citation: March J, Silva S, Petrycki S, et al. "Fluoxetine, Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy, and Their Combination for Adolescents with Depression: Treatment for Adolescents with Depression Study (TADS) Randomized Controlled Trial." JAMA. 2004;292(7):807–820. doi:10.1001/jama.292.7.807. PubMed: 15315995
papers.practice_changing: Yes — guides adolescent depression treatment.
papers.why_matters: TADS (N=439, ages 12–17) established that combination treatment (fluoxetine + CBT) is the most effective approach for adolescent depression (71% response vs. 61% fluoxetine alone, 43% CBT alone, 35% placebo). Critically, CBT appeared to protect against treatment-emergent suicidality — suicidal events were twice as common with fluoxetine alone compared to combination or CBT alone.[49][59]
papers.key_findings: Combination effect size 0.98, fluoxetine 0.68, CBT −0.03. Remission: combination 37%, fluoxetine 23%, CBT 16%, placebo 17%.[49][60]
clinical_pearls: Combination treatment (medication + therapy) is the gold standard for adolescent depression
CBT alone was not superior to placebo at 12 weeks — medication is often necessary
CBT may protect against antidepressant-associated suicidality
Fluoxetine is the first-line antidepressant for adolescents (best evidence base)
Monitor closely for suicidal ideation, especially in the first 4–8 weeks
papers.recommended_follow_up: March & Vitiello. "Clinical Messages from the Treatment for Adolescents with Depression Study (TADS)." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2009.[61]

papers.short_title: Zarate et al. — Ketamine for Treatment-Resistant Depression
papers.primary_citation: Zarate CA, Singh JB, Carlson PJ, et al. "A Randomized Trial of an N-methyl-D-aspartate Antagonist in Treatment-Resistant Major Depression." Archives of General Psychiatry. 2006;63(8):856–864. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.63.8.856. PubMed: 16894061
papers.practice_changing: Yes — launched the rapid-acting antidepressant era.
papers.why_matters: This proof-of-concept crossover RCT (N=18) demonstrated that a single IV infusion of ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) produced rapid antidepressant effects within 2 hours in treatment-resistant MDD, with ~71% response and ~29% remission at 24 hours lasting up to 7 days. This opened an entirely new chapter in antidepressant research by demonstrating that the glutamate system — not just monoamines — could be targeted for rapid antidepressant effects, ultimately leading to FDA approval of intranasal esketamine in 2019.[62][63]
papers.key_findings: Rapid onset (2 hours), large effect size, ~71% response at 24 hours. Effects lasted up to 7 days. The ELEKT-D trial (2023) subsequently showed ketamine was noninferior to ECT for treatment-resistant depression.[62][64]
clinical_pearls: Ketamine/esketamine represents a paradigm shift — rapid-acting antidepressants are now available
Esketamine (Spravato) is FDA-approved for TRD and MDD with acute suicidal ideation/behavior
Effects are rapid but transient — maintenance dosing strategies are still being optimized
Monitor for dissociation, blood pressure elevation, and abuse potential
The glutamate hypothesis complements (not replaces) the monoamine hypothesis
papers.recommended_follow_up: Anand et al. "Ketamine versus ECT for Nonpsychotic Treatment-Resistant Major Depression." NEJM. 2023.[64]

papers.short_title: Sackeim et al. — Post-ECT Relapse Prevention
papers.primary_citation: Sackeim HA, Haskett RF, Mulsant BH, et al. "Continuation Pharmacotherapy in the Prevention of Relapse Following Electroconvulsive Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial." JAMA. 2001;285(10):1299–1307. doi:10.1001/jama.285.10.1299. PubMed: 11255384
papers.practice_changing: Yes — post-ECT continuation treatment is standard of care.
papers.why_matters: This trial demonstrated that virtually all ECT remitters relapse without active continuation treatment (84% on placebo at 24 weeks), and that combination nortriptyline-lithium (39% relapse) was superior to nortriptyline alone (60%) or placebo. This established the imperative for post-ECT continuation pharmacotherapy and informed the CORE study showing continuation ECT is an equivalent alternative.[39][65]
papers.key_findings: Relapse rates: placebo 84%, nortriptyline 60%, nortriptyline-lithium 39%. Most relapses occurred in the first 4–6 weeks.[39]
clinical_pearls: Never discharge a patient after ECT without a continuation treatment plan
Nortriptyline-lithium combination or continuation ECT are the evidence-based options
The first 4–6 weeks post-ECT are the highest-risk period for relapse
Consider continuation ECT for patients who cannot tolerate pharmacotherapy or have relapsed on it
papers.recommended_follow_up: Kellner et al. "Continuation Electroconvulsive Therapy vs Pharmacotherapy for Relapse Prevention." Archives of General Psychiatry. 2006.[65]

papers.short_title: Fudala et al. — Office-Based Buprenorphine/Naloxone for Opioid Dependence
papers.primary_citation: Fudala PJ, Bridge TP, Herbert S, et al. "Office-Based Treatment of Opiate Addiction with a Sublingual-Tablet Formulation of Buprenorphine and Naloxone." New England Journal of Medicine. 2003;349(10):949–958. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa022164. PubMed: 12954743
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the foundation of office-based opioid treatment.
papers.why_matters: This pivotal multicenter RCT (N=326) was stopped early for efficacy, demonstrating that buprenorphine/naloxone was safe and effective for opioid dependence treatment in office-based settings. Opiate-negative urines were 17.8% (combination) vs. 5.8% (placebo, p<0.001). This trial was critical to the passage of DATA 2000 and the transformation of opioid addiction treatment from methadone clinics to primary care offices.[66]
papers.key_findings: Stopped early for efficacy. Both buprenorphine formulations significantly reduced opioid use and craving. Open-label phase showed 35–67% opiate-negative urines at 48–52 weeks.[66]
clinical_pearls: Buprenorphine can be safely prescribed in office-based settings — this is now standard of care
Buprenorphine/naloxone is preferred over buprenorphine alone to reduce diversion risk
Induction requires the patient to be in mild-moderate withdrawal (COWS ≥8–12)
Buprenorphine's ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes it safer than full agonists
The X-waiver requirement was eliminated in 2023, expanding prescribing access
papers.recommended_follow_up: Fiellin et al. "Counseling Plus Buprenorphine-Naloxone Maintenance Therapy for Opioid Dependence." NEJM. 2006.[67]

papers.short_title: Anton et al. — COMBINE Study (Alcohol Use Disorder)
papers.primary_citation: Anton RF, O'Malley SS, Ciraulo DA, et al. "Combined Pharmacotherapies and Behavioral Interventions for Alcohol Dependence: The COMBINE Study: A Randomized Controlled Trial." JAMA. 2006;295(17):2003–2017. doi:10.1001/jama.295.17.2003. PubMed: 16670409
papers.practice_changing: Yes — guides AUD pharmacotherapy selection.
papers.why_matters: The largest and most comprehensive pharmacotherapy trial for AUD (N=1,383, 9 arms, 11 sites) demonstrated that naltrexone 100 mg/day reduced heavy drinking (HR 0.72, p=0.02) and that medical management alone was a sufficient platform for medication delivery. Surprisingly, acamprosate showed no benefit — contradicting positive European trials. A significant naltrexone × behavioral intervention interaction showed that either naltrexone or combined behavioral intervention improved outcomes, but combining both did not add incremental benefit.[68]
papers.key_findings: All groups improved dramatically (percent days abstinent from 25% to 73%). Naltrexone effective; acamprosate not. Medical management sufficient for medication delivery.[68]
clinical_pearls: Naltrexone is effective for AUD and can be prescribed with brief medical management
Acamprosate's efficacy may depend on patient characteristics (longer pre-treatment abstinence)
Pharmacotherapy and behavioral intervention may be partially interchangeable — offer at least one
All patients improved substantially, highlighting the importance of any structured treatment contact
papers.recommended_follow_up: Jonas et al. "Pharmacotherapy for Adults with Alcohol Use Disorders in Outpatient Settings." JAMA. 2014.[69]

papers.short_title: Dole & Nyswander — Methadone Maintenance Treatment
papers.primary_citation: Dole VP, Nyswander M. "A Medical Treatment for Diacetylmorphine (Heroin) Addiction: A Clinical Trial with Methadone Hydrochloride." JAMA. 1965;193(8):646–650. doi:10.1001/jama.1965.03090080008002. PubMed: 14321530
papers.practice_changing: Yes — methadone remains the gold standard for severe OUD.
papers.why_matters: This foundational study of 22 heroin-addicted patients established methadone maintenance as the first effective medical treatment for opioid addiction, launching the modern era of medication-assisted treatment. By demonstrating that oral methadone could relieve craving, block heroin's effects, and enable social rehabilitation, Dole and Nyswander reframed addiction as a metabolic disease rather than a moral failing. A Cochrane review confirmed methadone maintenance increases treatment retention 4.4-fold compared to no opioid replacement.[70][71]
papers.key_findings: Methadone relieved narcotic craving, induced sufficient tolerance to block heroin, and enabled employment, education, and family reconciliation.[70]
clinical_pearls: Methadone maintenance is the most evidence-based treatment for severe opioid use disorder
Adequate dosing (≥60 mg/day, often 80–120 mg) is essential for efficacy
Methadone requires dispensing through licensed opioid treatment programs (OTPs)
QTc prolongation is a dose-dependent risk — obtain baseline ECG
The Kakko et al. (2003) trial showed 4 deaths in the placebo group vs. 0 with buprenorphine, demonstrating that opioid agonist treatment saves lives[72]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Mattick et al. "Buprenorphine Maintenance Versus Placebo or Methadone Maintenance for Opioid Dependence." Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014.[73]

papers.short_title: Barlow et al. — CBT vs. Imipramine for Panic Disorder
papers.primary_citation: Barlow DH, Gorman JM, Shear MK, Woods SW. "Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy, Imipramine, or Their Combination for Panic Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial." JAMA. 2000;283(19):2529–2536. doi:10.1001/jama.283.19.2529. PubMed: 10815116
papers.practice_changing: Yes — CBT remains first-line for panic disorder.
papers.why_matters: This definitive multicenter RCT (N=312) established that CBT and imipramine are comparably effective for panic disorder (49% vs. 46% response), with combination treatment showing a modest advantage (60%). Critically, CBT's effects were more durable — imipramine patients relapsed after discontinuation while CBT gains were maintained. This established CBT as the first-line treatment for panic disorder and demonstrated that psychotherapy can match pharmacotherapy for anxiety disorders.[74]
papers.key_findings: Response rates: CBT 49%, imipramine 46%, combination 60%, placebo 22%. CBT effects more durable after treatment discontinuation.[74]
clinical_pearls: CBT is the first-line treatment for panic disorder — it is as effective as medication with more durable effects
If medication is used, SSRIs are preferred over TCAs due to better tolerability
Benzodiazepines provide rapid relief but should not be first-line due to dependence risk
Exposure to feared situations is the active ingredient — avoidance maintains panic
A 2022 network meta-analysis of 136 RCTs confirmed CBT as the best-supported intervention for panic disorder[75]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Papola et al. "Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of Psychotherapies for Panic Disorder." British Journal of Psychiatry. 2022.[75]

papers.short_title: Resick et al. — Cognitive Processing Therapy for PTSD
papers.primary_citation: Resick PA, Nishith P, Weaver TL, Astin MC, Feuer CA. "A Comparison of Cognitive-Processing Therapy with Prolonged Exposure and a Waiting Condition for the Treatment of Chronic Posttraumatic Stress Disorder in Female Rape Victims." Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 2002;70(4):867–879. doi:10.1037/0022-006X.70.4.867. PubMed: 12182270
papers.practice_changing: Yes — CPT and PE are the standard of care for PTSD.
papers.why_matters: This RCT (N=171) established CPT as an evidence-based treatment for PTSD, demonstrating comparable efficacy to prolonged exposure. Both treatments were highly effective and superior to a waiting condition. Long-term follow-up (5–10 years) showed treatment gains were maintained, with only ~20% still meeting PTSD criteria. CPT and PE are now the two first-line psychotherapies recommended by the APA and VA/DoD guidelines.[76][77]
papers.key_findings: CPT and PE both produced large improvements; CPT showed better outcomes on guilt measures. At 5–10 year follow-up, gains were maintained.[76][77]
clinical_pearls: CPT and PE are the gold-standard psychotherapies for PTSD — both are strongly recommended
CPT focuses on challenging maladaptive cognitions ("stuck points") about the trauma
PE focuses on habituation through repeated imaginal and in vivo exposure
The largest head-to-head trial (N=916) found PE statistically but not clinically superior to CPT[78]
Dropout from trauma-focused therapies is high (35–56%) — engagement strategies are critical
papers.recommended_follow_up: Schnurr et al. "Comparison of Prolonged Exposure vs Cognitive Processing Therapy for Treatment of PTSD Among US Veterans." JAMA Network Open. 2022.[78]

papers.short_title: Brady et al. — Sertraline for PTSD
papers.primary_citation: Brady K, Pearlstein T, Asnis GM, et al. "Efficacy and Safety of Sertraline Treatment of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial." JAMA. 2000;283(14):1837–1844. doi:10.1001/jama.283.14.1837. PubMed: 10770145
papers.practice_changing: Yes — sertraline remains first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD.
papers.why_matters: This landmark 12-week RCT (N=187) established sertraline as an effective pharmacotherapy for PTSD (53% vs. 32% response, p=0.008), contributing to its FDA approval — one of only two medications (with paroxetine) approved for PTSD. The Cochrane review confirmed SSRIs as a class are effective for PTSD (RR 0.66 for response).[79][80]
papers.key_findings: Sertraline produced significantly greater improvement on CAPS-2 (−33.0 vs. −23.2, p=0.02). Response rate 53% vs. 32% (p=0.008).[79]
clinical_pearls: Sertraline and paroxetine are the only FDA-approved medications for PTSD
SSRIs have smaller effect sizes in PTSD (~0.25) than in depression or anxiety disorders
Trauma-focused psychotherapy is generally preferred over pharmacotherapy for PTSD
Prazosin may help with PTSD-related nightmares (though evidence is mixed)
Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD and may worsen outcomes
papers.recommended_follow_up: Williams et al. "Pharmacotherapy for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)." Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022.[80]

papers.short_title: POTS — Pediatric OCD Treatment Study
papers.primary_citation: Pediatric OCD Treatment Study (POTS) Team. "Cognitive-Behavior Therapy, Sertraline, and Their Combination for Children and Adolescents with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder." JAMA. 2004;292(16):1969–1976. doi:10.1001/jama.292.16.1969. PubMed: 15507582
papers.practice_changing: Yes — guides pediatric OCD treatment.
papers.why_matters: This NIMH-funded RCT (N=112, ages 7–17) demonstrated that combination CBT + sertraline was superior to either monotherapy for pediatric OCD (remission: 53.6% vs. 39.3% CBT vs. 21.4% sertraline vs. 3.6% placebo). CBT alone and sertraline alone did not differ from each other. This established the treatment algorithm for pediatric OCD: start with combination or CBT alone.[81]
papers.key_findings: Combination > monotherapy > placebo. CBT alone was as effective as sertraline alone. Placebo remission was only 3.6%, confirming OCD's low spontaneous remission rate.[81]
clinical_pearls: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the core CBT technique for OCD
SSRIs for OCD require higher doses and longer trials (8–12 weeks) than for depression
Combination treatment is optimal; if choosing one modality, CBT is preferred
OCD has a very low placebo response rate — if symptoms improve, it is likely treatment effect
The NNT for SSRIs in OCD is approximately 5[82]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Hirschtritt et al. "Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: Advances in Diagnosis and Treatment." JAMA. 2017.[82]

papers.short_title: Huhn et al. — Comparative Efficacy of 32 Antipsychotics
papers.primary_citation: Huhn M, Nikolakopoulou A, Schneider-Thoma J, et al. "Comparative Efficacy and Tolerability of 32 Oral Antipsychotics for the Acute Treatment of Adults with Multi-Episode Schizophrenia." Lancet. 2019;394(10202):939–951. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31135-3. PubMed: 31303314
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the definitive antipsychotic comparison reference.
papers.why_matters: The largest network meta-analysis in schizophrenia (402 studies, 53,463 participants, 32 antipsychotics) confirmed that clozapine remains the most efficacious antipsychotic (SMD −0.89) and that side-effect differences are more marked than efficacy differences. Only clozapine, amisulpride, zotepine, olanzapine, and risperidone were significantly more efficacious than other antipsychotics.[2]
papers.key_findings: SMDs ranged from −0.89 (clozapine) to −0.03 (levomepromazine). Weight gain ranged from −0.16 kg (ziprasidone) to 3.21 kg (zotepine).[2]
clinical_pearls: Antipsychotic selection should be driven primarily by side-effect profile, not efficacy (except clozapine)
The FGA/SGA classification is pharmacologically meaningless — individual drugs vary more within classes than between them
Clozapine stands alone as the most efficacious agent — it should not be withheld from eligible patients
papers.recommended_follow_up: Schneider-Thoma et al. "Comparative Efficacy and Tolerability of 32 Oral and Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotics for the Maintenance Treatment of Adults with Schizophrenia." Lancet. 2022.[83]

papers.short_title: Tiihonen et al. — FIN11 Mortality Study
papers.primary_citation: Tiihonen J, Lönnqvist J, Wahlbeck K, et al. "11-Year Follow-Up of Mortality in Patients with Schizophrenia: A Population-Based Cohort Study (FIN11 Study)." Lancet. 2009;374(9690):620–627. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60742-X. PubMed: 19595447
papers.practice_changing: Yes — counters the narrative that antipsychotics are harmful long-term.
papers.why_matters: This population-based cohort of 66,881 Finnish patients with schizophrenia (11-year follow-up) overturned the prevailing narrative that antipsychotics shorten life. Long-term antipsychotic use was associated with lower mortality than no use, and clozapine was associated with the lowest mortality (−26% vs. perphenazine). The 20-year follow-up confirmed these findings: cumulative mortality was 46.2% without antipsychotics vs. 15.6% with clozapine.[84][6]
papers.key_findings: Antipsychotic use reduced mortality. Clozapine had the lowest mortality. Quetiapine and haloperidol were associated with increased mortality vs. perphenazine.[84]
clinical_pearls: Antipsychotics save lives in schizophrenia — the mortality benefit is substantial
Clozapine is associated with the lowest mortality despite its metabolic side effects
The cardiovascular mortality reduction likely reflects improved self-care, reduced substance use, and reduced suicide
These data support long-term antipsychotic treatment as life-prolonging, not life-shortening
papers.recommended_follow_up: Taipale et al. "20-Year Follow-Up Study of Physical Morbidity and Mortality in Relationship to Antipsychotic Treatment." World Psychiatry. 2020.[6]

papers.short_title: Elkin et al. — NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program
papers.primary_citation: Elkin I, Shea MT, Watkins JT, et al. "National Institute of Mental Health Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program: General Effectiveness of Treatments." Archives of General Psychiatry. 1989;46(11):971–982. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.1989.01810110013002. PubMed: 2684085
papers.practice_changing: Partially — methodology remains influential; specific findings have been refined.
papers.why_matters: The first large-scale multisite RCT comparing psychotherapy (CBT and IPT) to pharmacotherapy (imipramine) and placebo for MDD (N=239). All active treatments produced significant improvement with few overall differences, though imipramine showed advantages in more severely depressed patients. This trial established the methodology for psychotherapy research and launched decades of debate about the relative merits of psychotherapy vs. pharmacotherapy.[85][86]
papers.key_findings: All active treatments effective. Few differences overall. Imipramine possibly superior for severe depression (later challenged by Weitz et al. 2015 IPD meta-analysis showing no severity moderation).[85][87]
clinical_pearls: Psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are comparably effective for mild-moderate depression
For severe depression, combination treatment is generally recommended
The "Dodo bird verdict" — that all bona fide psychotherapies are roughly equivalent — has substantial empirical support[88]
Treatment selection should consider patient preference, availability, and comorbidities
papers.recommended_follow_up: Cuijpers et al. "Cognitive Behavior Therapy vs. Control Conditions, Other Psychotherapies, Pharmacotherapies and Combined Treatment for Depression." World Psychiatry. 2023.[89]

papers.short_title: Flückiger et al. — Therapeutic Alliance Meta-Analysis
papers.primary_citation: Flückiger C, Del Re AC, Wampold BE, Horvath AO. "The Alliance in Adult Psychotherapy: A Meta-Analytic Synthesis." Psychotherapy. 2018;55(4):316–340. doi:10.1037/pst0000172. PubMed: 30335440
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the therapeutic relationship is central to all psychiatric care.
papers.why_matters: This definitive meta-analysis (295 studies, >30,000 patients, 1978–2017) confirmed that the therapeutic alliance is a robust, consistent predictor of psychotherapy outcomes across all treatment approaches (r = .278, d = 0.579). The relationship held regardless of alliance scale, rater, treatment type, patient characteristics, or country. This is the strongest evidence that the quality of the therapeutic relationship matters as much as — or more than — the specific technique used.[90]
papers.key_findings: Alliance-outcome correlation r = .278 (95% CI .256–.299). Consistent across treatment approaches, patient characteristics, and countries. Also applies to internet-based psychotherapy (r = .275).[90]
clinical_pearls: The therapeutic alliance is the single strongest predictor of psychotherapy outcomes
Alliance comprises three elements: agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and the therapeutic bond (Bordin 1979)
Building alliance is a clinical skill that can be taught and improved
A strong alliance does not mean avoiding difficult conversations — it means having them within a trusting relationship
Therapist variability in alliance formation is more important than patient variability for outcomes[91]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Wampold & Flückiger. "The Alliance in Mental Health Care: Conceptualization, Evidence and Clinical Applications." World Psychiatry. 2023.[92]

papers.short_title: Miller & Rollnick — Motivational Interviewing / Project MATCH
papers.primary_citation: Project MATCH Research Group. "Matching Alcoholism Treatments to Client Heterogeneity: Project MATCH Posttreatment Drinking Outcomes." Journal of Studies on Alcohol. 1997;58(1):7–29. PubMed: 8979210
papers.practice_changing: Yes — MI is a foundational clinical skill.
papers.why_matters: The largest psychosocial treatment trial for alcoholism (N=1,726) compared CBT, Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MET, 4 sessions), and Twelve-Step Facilitation. All three treatments produced significant, sustained improvements with no major differences between them. The primary matching hypothesis was largely unsupported. MET's comparable effectiveness in only 4 sessions (vs. 12 for CBT/TSF) demonstrated the power of motivational interviewing as a brief intervention. At 3-year follow-up, ~30% remained totally abstinent.[93][94][95]
papers.key_findings: All treatments effective; no major differences. MET achieved comparable outcomes in one-third the sessions. Matching hypotheses largely unsupported.[93][95]
clinical_pearls: Motivational interviewing is effective and efficient — even brief interventions produce meaningful change
The spirit of MI (partnership, acceptance, compassion, evocation) is more important than specific techniques
"Rolling with resistance" rather than confronting it is more effective for behavior change
MI skills are applicable across all of psychiatry, not just substance use disorders
Any structured treatment contact improves outcomes — the specific modality matters less than engagement
papers.recommended_follow_up: Schwenker et al. "Motivational Interviewing for Substance Use Reduction." Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023.[96]

papers.short_title: Ely et al. — CAM-ICU Validation
papers.primary_citation: Ely EW, Inouye SK, Bernard GR, et al. "Delirium in Mechanically Ventilated Patients: Validity and Reliability of the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU)." JAMA. 2001;286(21):2703–2710. doi:10.1001/jama.286.21.2703. PubMed: 11730446
papers.practice_changing: Yes — standard ICU delirium screening tool.
papers.why_matters: The CAM-ICU adapted the original CAM for use in mechanically ventilated and nonverbal patients, achieving sensitivity 93–100% and specificity 98–100% in 2 minutes. Delirium occurred in 83% of ICU patients. This tool is now one of two delirium screening instruments recommended by the SCCM PADIS guidelines and is used in ICUs worldwide.[97][98]
papers.key_findings: Sensitivity 93–100%, specificity 98–100%, interrater reliability κ = 0.96. Mean administration time 2 minutes. Delirium prevalence 83% in mechanically ventilated patients.[97]
clinical_pearls: Delirium is the norm, not the exception, in ICU patients — screen routinely
The CAM-ICU can be performed in nonverbal, intubated patients
ICU delirium is independently associated with increased mortality, longer ICU stay, and long-term cognitive impairment
Nonpharmacologic prevention (ABCDEF bundle) is the primary intervention
papers.recommended_follow_up: Devlin et al. "Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Management of Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, and Sleep Disruption in Adult Patients in the ICU." Critical Care Medicine. 2018.[98]

papers.short_title: Guo et al. — Measurement-Based Care for Depression
papers.primary_citation: Guo T, Xiang YT, Xiao L, et al. "Measurement-Based Care Versus Standard Care for Major Depression: A Randomized Controlled Trial with Blind Raters." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2015;172(10):1004–1013. doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.2015.14050652. PubMed: 25869507
papers.practice_changing: Yes — MBC is now the standard of care for depression treatment.
papers.why_matters: This RCT (N=120) provided the most compelling evidence that measurement-based care (MBC) — systematic monitoring of symptoms using validated scales to guide treatment decisions — dramatically improves depression outcomes. MBC achieved 73.8% remission vs. 28.8% with standard care, and halved the time to remission (10.2 vs. 19.2 weeks). A meta-analysis of 7 RCTs confirmed MBC's superiority (OR 1.83 for remission).[99][100]
papers.key_findings: Remission 73.8% vs. 28.8%; response 86.9% vs. 62.7%; time to remission 10.2 vs. 19.2 weeks.[99]
clinical_pearls: Use the PHQ-9 or QIDS at every visit to track depression severity and guide treatment decisions
MBC ensures adequate dosing, timely switching, and appropriate augmentation
The Joint Commission has required MBC in accredited behavioral health programs since 2018[63]
MBC is not just "checking a box" — it fundamentally changes clinical decision-making
papers.recommended_follow_up: Trivedi. "How Can Measurement-Based Care Help Improve Treatment Outcomes for Major Depressive Disorder in Primary Care?" Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2020.[101]

papers.short_title: Stanley & Brown — Safety Planning Intervention
papers.primary_citation: Stanley B, Brown GK, Brenner LA, et al. "Comparison of the Safety Planning Intervention with Follow-Up vs Usual Care of Suicidal Patients Treated in the Emergency Department." JAMA Psychiatry. 2018;75(9):894–900. doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2018.1776. PubMed: 29998307
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the standard brief suicide prevention intervention.
papers.why_matters: This large cohort comparison (N=1,640 veterans, 9 EDs) demonstrated that the Safety Planning Intervention with follow-up (SPI+) was associated with 45% fewer suicidal behaviors (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.33–0.95) and more than doubled outpatient treatment engagement (OR 2.06) over 6 months post-ED discharge. The SPI has become the most widely implemented brief suicide prevention intervention in healthcare settings and is a Best Practice on the SPRC/AFSP registry.[1]
papers.key_findings: Suicidal behavior: 3.03% (SPI+) vs. 5.29% (usual care). The SPI's 6 steps — warning signs, internal coping, social contacts for distraction, people to contact for help, professionals/crisis services, and lethal means counseling — provide a structured, personalized crisis roadmap.[1]
clinical_pearls: Every suicidal patient discharged from the ED or inpatient unit should have a written safety plan
Safety plans are NOT "no-suicide contracts" — contracts lack evidence and may be coercive[2]
The SPI takes 20–45 minutes and can be completed by any trained clinician
Follow-up contact within 72 hours of discharge is a critical component
Two-thirds of patients who receive a safety plan report using it during subsequent crises[1]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Doupnik et al. "Association of Suicide Prevention Interventions with Subsequent Suicide Attempts." JAMA Psychiatry. 2020.[3]

papers.short_title: Schneider et al. — CATIE-AD (Antipsychotics in Dementia)
papers.primary_citation: Schneider LS, Tariot PN, Dagerman KS, et al. "Effectiveness of Atypical Antipsychotic Drugs in Patients with Alzheimer's Disease." New England Journal of Medicine. 2006;355(15):1525–1538. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa061240. PubMed: 17035647
papers.practice_changing: Yes — shapes every antipsychotic prescription in dementia.
papers.why_matters: This NIMH-funded trial (N=421) randomized AD outpatients with psychosis or agitation to olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, or placebo. The primary finding was that adverse effects offset any advantages — no antipsychotic was superior to placebo for time to discontinuation for any reason. Cognitive function declined more with antipsychotics than placebo (MMSE −2.4 points over 36 weeks), equivalent to approximately one year of additional cognitive deterioration. Combined with the FDA black box warning on antipsychotic mortality in dementia (OR 1.54 for death), this trial fundamentally changed the risk-benefit calculus for antipsychotic use in dementia.[4][5]
papers.key_findings: Median time to discontinuation: quetiapine 5.3 weeks, olanzapine 7.1, risperidone 7.4, placebo 8.0. NNH for mortality with antipsychotics in dementia: haloperidol 26, risperidone 27, quetiapine 50 over 180 days.[4][6]
clinical_pearls: Antipsychotics in dementia carry a black box warning for increased mortality (~1.6–1.7× risk)
Nonpharmacologic interventions should always be tried first for BPSD
If antipsychotics are used, start low, go slow, and plan for regular reassessment and discontinuation attempts
Cognitive decline accelerates with antipsychotic use in dementia patients
Document the risk-benefit discussion and obtain informed consent
papers.recommended_follow_up: Tampi & Jeste. "Dementia Is More Than Memory Loss." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2022.[7]

papers.short_title: Nasreddine et al. — Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)
papers.primary_citation: Nasreddine ZS, Phillips NA, Bédirian V, et al. "The Montreal Cognitive Assessment, MoCA: A Brief Screening Tool for Mild Cognitive Impairment." Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2005;53(4):695–699. doi:10.1111/j.1532-5415.2005.53221.x. PubMed: 15817019
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the standard cognitive screening tool.
papers.why_matters: The MoCA was developed to address the MMSE's poor sensitivity for mild cognitive impairment. In the original validation (N=277), the MoCA detected 90% of MCI subjects versus only 18% for the MMSE, while maintaining 87% specificity. It assesses executive function, visuospatial ability, and verbal fluency more thoroughly than the MMSE and has become the preferred cognitive screening tool in most clinical settings.[1][8]
papers.key_findings: MoCA sensitivity for MCI: 90% (vs. MMSE 18%); for mild AD: 100% (vs. MMSE 78%). Optimal cutoff may be ≤23 rather than the original ≤25.[1][9]
clinical_pearls: The MoCA is superior to the MMSE for detecting MCI and should be the default cognitive screen
Takes ~10 minutes; freely available for clinical use
Add 1 point for ≤12 years of education
Executive function items (trail-making, clock drawing, verbal fluency) are particularly sensitive to early cognitive decline
Always interpret in context — depression, delirium, and education level affect scores
papers.recommended_follow_up: Arvanitakis et al. "Diagnosis and Management of Dementia: Review." JAMA. 2019.[10]

papers.short_title: Reisberg et al. — Memantine for Moderate-to-Severe Alzheimer's Disease
papers.primary_citation: Reisberg B, Doody R, Stöffler A, et al. "Memantine in Moderate-to-Severe Alzheimer's Disease." New England Journal of Medicine. 2003;348(14):1333–1341. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa013128. PubMed: 12672860
papers.practice_changing: Yes — memantine remains standard of care for moderate-to-severe AD.
papers.why_matters: This landmark 28-week RCT (N=252) established memantine as the first treatment for moderate-to-severe AD, demonstrating less functional and cognitive decline compared to placebo. Response rate was 29% vs. 10% (p<0.001). Memantine introduced a novel NMDA-receptor-based mechanism distinct from cholinesterase inhibitors, and the subsequent Tariot et al. (2004) trial showed benefit of adding memantine to donepezil.[11][12]
papers.key_findings: Memantine showed less deterioration on SIB (p<0.001), ADCS-ADLsev (p=0.02), and CIBIC-plus (p=0.03). Cochrane review confirmed small but consistent benefits (SMD −0.27 for cognition).[11][13]
clinical_pearls: Memantine is indicated for moderate-to-severe AD (MMSE <15) — it does not replace ChEIs
Can be combined with donepezil for additive benefit
Well tolerated with minimal side effects compared to ChEIs
Benefits are modest — set realistic expectations with families
ChEIs (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) improve ADAS-cog by ~2.4 points — statistically significant but of uncertain clinical importance[14]
papers.recommended_follow_up: McShane et al. "Memantine for Dementia." Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019.[13]

papers.short_title: Miklowitz et al. — Family-Focused Therapy for Bipolar Disorder
papers.primary_citation: Miklowitz DJ, George EL, Richards JA, Simoneau TL, Suddath RL. "A Randomized Study of Family-Focused Psychoeducation and Pharmacotherapy in the Outpatient Management of Bipolar Disorder." Archives of General Psychiatry. 2003;60(9):904–912. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.60.9.904. PubMed: 12963672
papers.practice_changing: Yes — family psychoeducation is a guideline-recommended intervention.
papers.why_matters: This RCT (N=101) demonstrated that Family-Focused Therapy (FFT) — 21 sessions of psychoeducation, communication enhancement, and problem-solving skills training — significantly reduced relapse rates and improved medication adherence in bipolar disorder compared to crisis management. A 2022 network meta-analysis of family interventions in schizophrenia confirmed that family psychoeducation reduces relapse from 37% to 10% at 12 months.[15]
papers.key_findings: FFT patients had fewer relapses, longer survival intervals, and better medication adherence over 2 years. The STEP-BD psychotherapy companion study confirmed that intensive psychotherapy (including FFT) improved recovery rates to 64% vs. 52%.[16]
clinical_pearls: Family psychoeducation reduces relapse in both bipolar disorder and schizophrenia
High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement) predicts relapse — family interventions target this
Even simple psychoeducation (12 sessions) is effective — complex interventions are not always necessary[15]
Family involvement should be offered to all patients with serious mental illness, not just those in crisis
The NAMI Family-to-Family program is a widely available community resource
papers.recommended_follow_up: Rodolico et al. "Family Interventions for Relapse Prevention in Schizophrenia: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis." Lancet Psychiatry. 2022.[15]

papers.short_title: Cuijpers et al. — Psychotherapy for Depression Meta-Analysis
papers.primary_citation: Cuijpers P, Miguel C, Harrer M, et al. "Cognitive Behavior Therapy vs. Control Conditions, Other Psychotherapies, Pharmacotherapies and Combined Treatment for Depression: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis Including 409 Trials with 52,702 Patients." World Psychiatry. 2023;22(1):105–115. doi:10.1002/wps.21069. PubMed: 36640389
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the definitive psychotherapy evidence base.
papers.why_matters: The most comprehensive meta-analysis of psychotherapy for depression ever conducted (409 RCTs, 52,702 patients) confirmed that CBT is effective compared to all control conditions (g=0.75), with no significant differences between CBT and other bona fide psychotherapies (behavioral activation, interpersonal therapy, psychodynamic therapy, problem-solving therapy). Combined treatment (CBT + pharmacotherapy) was superior to either alone. This provides the definitive evidence base for psychotherapy in depression.[17]
papers.key_findings: CBT vs. controls: g=0.75. CBT vs. other psychotherapies: no significant differences. Combined treatment > monotherapy. Effects maintained at follow-up.[17]
clinical_pearls: All evidence-based psychotherapies for depression are roughly equally effective
Combined treatment (medication + therapy) is superior to either alone
The specific therapy matters less than whether the patient receives any structured treatment
Behavioral activation is as effective as full CBT and may be easier to disseminate
Patient preference should guide psychotherapy selection
papers.recommended_follow_up: Cuijpers et al. "Psychotherapies for Depression: A Network Meta-Analysis." World Psychiatry. 2021.[18]

papers.short_title: Anthony — Recovery Model in Mental Health
papers.primary_citation: Anthony WA. "Recovery from Mental Illness: The Guiding Vision of the Mental Health Service System in the 1990s." Psychosocial Rehabilitation Journal. 1993;16(4):11–23. doi:10.1037/h0095655.
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the recovery model is the philosophical foundation of modern mental health services.
papers.why_matters: This seminal paper articulated the recovery model as the guiding vision for mental health services, defining recovery as "a deeply personal, unique process of changing one's attitudes, values, feelings, goals, skills, and/or roles... a way of living a satisfying, hopeful, and contributing life even with limitations caused by illness." This reframed the goal of psychiatric treatment from symptom elimination to meaningful life participation. The CHIME framework (Connectedness, Hope, Identity, Meaning, Empowerment) subsequently operationalized recovery processes, and SAMHSA adopted recovery as a central organizing principle.[9][19]
papers.key_findings: Recovery is possible even without complete symptom remission. Recovery is person-driven, not clinician-driven. The mental health system should be organized around recovery principles.[9]
clinical_pearls: Ask patients about their goals, not just their symptoms — recovery is about living a meaningful life
Hope is therapeutic — communicate realistic optimism about outcomes
Peer support specialists are evidence-based recovery resources
Recovery-oriented care emphasizes autonomy, self-determination, and community integration
The recovery model does not reject medication — it rejects the idea that medication is sufficient
papers.recommended_follow_up: Winsper et al. "How Do Recovery-Oriented Interventions Contribute to Personal Mental Health Recovery?" Clinical Psychology Review. 2020.[20]

papers.short_title: Hamann et al. — Shared Decision Making in Psychiatry
papers.primary_citation: Hamann J, Leucht S, Kissling W. "Shared Decision Making in Psychiatry." Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica. 2003;107(6):403–409. doi:10.1034/j.1600-0447.2003.00130.x. PubMed: 12752015
papers.practice_changing: Yes — SDM is now a core principle of psychiatric care.
papers.why_matters: This influential paper introduced the shared decision-making (SDM) framework to psychiatry, arguing that even patients with serious mental illness can and should participate in treatment decisions. A 2022 Cochrane review of SDM interventions in mental health (14 RCTs) found that SDM improved patient satisfaction, knowledge, and treatment engagement, though effects on clinical outcomes were less consistent. SDM is now endorsed by NICE, WFSBP, and APA guidelines as a core component of recovery-oriented care.[19]
papers.key_findings: Most psychiatric patients want to be involved in treatment decisions. SDM improves the therapeutic relationship and may improve adherence. Barriers include clinician assumptions about patient capacity and time constraints.[19][21]
clinical_pearls: Shared decision making is an ethical imperative, not just a nice-to-have
Even patients with psychosis can participate meaningfully in treatment decisions
SDM involves three steps: information exchange, deliberation, and agreement on a plan
Use decision aids when available — they improve patient knowledge and reduce decisional conflict
SDM does not mean the patient decides alone — it means the clinician and patient decide together
papers.recommended_follow_up: Aoki et al. "Shared Decision-Making Interventions for People with Mental Health Conditions." Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022.[19]

papers.short_title: Kirkbride et al. — Social Determinants of Mental Health
papers.primary_citation: Kirkbride JB, Anglin DM, Colman I, et al. "The Social Determinants of Mental Health and Disorder: Evidence, Prevention and Recommendations." World Psychiatry. 2024;23(1):58–90. doi:10.1002/wps.21160. PubMed: 38214615
papers.practice_changing: Yes — increasingly integrated into psychiatric training and practice.
papers.why_matters: This comprehensive WPA review synthesized the evidence linking social determinants — poverty, racism, housing instability, adverse childhood experiences, migration, and LGBTQ+ minority stress — to mental health outcomes across the life course. It established a preventive framework and provided seven key recommendations for research, policy, and public health action. An umbrella review of 26 meta-analyses confirmed that childhood abuse, intimate partner violence, and food insecurity are associated with medium-effect-size increases in MDD risk.[22][23]
papers.key_findings: Social causation and social drift create a vicious cycle. Poverty alleviation, anti-discrimination policies, and trauma-informed care can interrupt this cycle. Modifiable social determinants account for a substantial proportion of mental disorder burden.[22][24]
clinical_pearls: Screen for social determinants (housing, food security, safety, financial stress) as part of psychiatric assessment
Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are dose-dependently associated with adult mental illness
Structural racism is a social determinant of mental health — acknowledge it in clinical practice
Social prescribing (connecting patients to community resources) is an emerging intervention
Addressing social determinants is not "outside the scope" of psychiatry — it is central to it
papers.recommended_follow_up: Alegría et al. "Recent Advances on Social Determinants of Mental Health." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2023.[25]

papers.short_title: Bowden et al. — Divalproex for Acute Mania
papers.primary_citation: Bowden CL, Brugger AM, Swann AC, et al. "Efficacy of Divalproex vs Lithium and Placebo in the Treatment of Mania." JAMA. 1994;271(12):918–924. doi:10.1001/jama.1994.03510360044034. PubMed: 8120960
papers.practice_changing: Partially — still used for acute mania, but lithium preferred for maintenance.
papers.why_matters: This pivotal multicenter RCT (N=179) established divalproex as an effective treatment for acute mania, with comparable efficacy to lithium (48% vs. 49% response) and superior tolerability. Divalproex was particularly effective in patients with mixed episodes and rapid cycling — populations that respond poorly to lithium. This trial led to FDA approval and made valproate the most prescribed mood stabilizer in the US for acute mania.
papers.key_findings: Divalproex response 48%, lithium 49%, placebo 25%. Divalproex better tolerated than lithium. Particularly effective for mixed states and rapid cycling.
clinical_pearls: Divalproex is effective for acute mania but inferior to lithium for maintenance (BALANCE trial)[26]
Loading dose strategy (20 mg/kg/day) can achieve therapeutic levels rapidly
Monitor hepatic function, CBC, and valproic acid levels
Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental effects)
For maintenance, lithium should generally be preferred over valproate
papers.recommended_follow_up: Yatham et al. "CANMAT and ISBD 2018 Guidelines for Management of Patients with Bipolar Disorder." Bipolar Disorders. 2018.

papers.short_title: Delay & Deniker — Discovery of Chlorpromazine
papers.primary_citation: Delay J, Deniker P. "Le traitement des psychoses par une méthode neurolytique dérivée de l'hibernothérapie." Comptes Rendus du Congrès des Médecins Aliénistes et Neurologistes de France. 1952;50:497–502.
papers.practice_changing: Historical only — but the most important historical paper in psychopharmacology.
papers.why_matters: This 1952 report described the first systematic use of chlorpromazine for psychosis, launching the psychopharmacological revolution. Delay and Deniker demonstrated that chlorpromazine could specifically treat psychotic symptoms — not merely sedate patients — fundamentally transforming psychiatry from a custodial to a therapeutic discipline. This discovery enabled deinstitutionalization and established the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia.
papers.key_findings: Chlorpromazine produced specific antipsychotic effects distinct from sedation. Patients with chronic psychosis showed dramatic improvement. The concept of "neuroleptic" action was introduced.
clinical_pearls: The discovery of chlorpromazine is the single most important event in the history of psychopharmacology
It established that psychiatric disorders have neurochemical substrates amenable to pharmacological intervention
