The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia emerged from understanding chlorpromazine's mechanism
All subsequent antipsychotic development builds on this foundation
Historical context: before chlorpromazine, the main treatments for psychosis were insulin coma, lobotomy, and restraint
papers.recommended_follow_up: Ban. "Fifty Years Chlorpromazine: A Historical Perspective." Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. 2007.

papers.short_title: Engel — The Biopsychosocial Model
papers.primary_citation: Engel GL. "The Need for a New Medical Model: A Challenge for Biomedicine." Science. 1977;196(4286):129–136. doi:10.1126/science.847460. PubMed: 847460
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the foundational conceptual model of psychiatry.
papers.why_matters: Engel's biopsychosocial model challenged the reductionist biomedical model by arguing that biological, psychological, and social factors all contribute to health and illness. This framework became the philosophical foundation of modern psychiatry and is explicitly taught in every medical school. While criticized for being vague and unfalsifiable, no alternative framework has replaced it, and it remains the dominant conceptual model for understanding mental illness.
papers.key_findings: The biomedical model is insufficient for understanding illness. Psychological and social factors are not merely "complications" but integral to disease causation and treatment. A systems-based approach is needed.
clinical_pearls: Every psychiatric formulation should address biological, psychological, and social factors
The biopsychosocial model is not just a checklist — it is a way of thinking about patients as whole persons
Treatment plans should address all three domains, not just pharmacotherapy
The model reminds us that social context (poverty, trauma, relationships) shapes mental illness
Critics argue the model needs updating — but no better integrative framework exists
papers.recommended_follow_up: Bolton & Gillett. "The Biopsychosocial Model of Health and Disease." Palgrave Macmillan, 2019.

papers.short_title: Rosenhan — "On Being Sane in Insane Places"
papers.primary_citation: Rosenhan DL. "On Being Sane in Insane Places." Science. 1973;179(4070):250–258. doi:10.1126/science.179.4070.250. PubMed: 4683124
papers.practice_changing: Historical only — but profoundly shaped modern diagnostic practices and patient rights.
papers.why_matters: Rosenhan's pseudopatient experiment — in which 8 sane individuals were admitted to psychiatric hospitals by reporting auditory hallucinations, then behaved normally but were not detected as sane — exposed the unreliability of psychiatric diagnosis and the dehumanizing effects of institutionalization. While methodologically controversial (and recently challenged by Cahalan's 2019 investigation), this study catalyzed the movement toward operationalized diagnostic criteria (DSM-III, 1980) and patient rights reforms.
papers.key_findings: All pseudopatients were admitted (7 with schizophrenia, 1 with manic-depressive psychosis). Length of stay ranged from 7–52 days. Staff never detected the pseudopatients; other patients did. Normal behaviors were interpreted through the lens of the diagnosis.
clinical_pearls: Diagnostic labels powerfully shape how clinicians perceive patient behavior — be aware of confirmation bias
The context of observation matters — behavior that seems pathological in a hospital may be normal outside it
This study directly contributed to the development of operationalized diagnostic criteria (DSM-III)
Psychiatric patients deserve the same dignity and respect as all other patients
The study's limitations (deception, small sample, no control group) are themselves educational
papers.recommended_follow_up: Cahalan. "The Great Pretender." Grand Central Publishing, 2019.

papers.short_title: van Dyck et al. — CLARITY-AD (Lecanemab for Early Alzheimer's Disease)
papers.primary_citation: van Dyck CH, Swanson CJ, Aisen P, et al. "Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease." New England Journal of Medicine. 2023;388(1):9–21. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2212948. PubMed: 36449413
papers.practice_changing: Yes — the first disease-modifying AD therapy, though clinical impact is still being defined.
papers.why_matters: The CLARITY-AD trial (N=1,795) was the first phase 3 trial to demonstrate that an anti-amyloid antibody (lecanemab) could slow clinical decline in early AD, with a 27% reduction in CDR-SB decline over 18 months (difference −0.45 points, p<0.001). All secondary endpoints favored lecanemab. This led to the first traditional FDA approval of an anti-amyloid therapy (July 2023) and validated the amyloid hypothesis after decades of failed trials. The clinical meaningfulness of the effect size remains debated.[27]
papers.key_findings: CDR-SB: 27% less decline. ADAS-cog14: −1.44 points. Amyloid reduction: −59.1 centiloids. ARIA-E: 12.6% vs. 1.7%. ARIA-H: 17.3% vs. 9.0%.[27]
clinical_pearls: Lecanemab represents the first disease-modifying therapy for AD — a paradigm shift
Requires amyloid PET or CSF confirmation before treatment
ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities) requires MRI monitoring — higher risk with APOE4 homozygosity
The ~0.45-point CDR-SB difference is statistically significant but clinically modest — counsel families accordingly
Donanemab (approved 2024) showed similar or slightly larger effects, particularly in low/medium tau patients[28][29]
papers.recommended_follow_up: Serrano-Pozo et al. "Alzheimer's Disease." Lancet. 2026.[28]
